task_row_model.query: In longitudinal observational studies with time-varying treatments and confounders that are themselves affected by prior treatment, when should one use marginal structural models estimated via inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) versus the parametric g-formula? Explain model specification, estimation steps, key assumptions (including positivity and exchangeability), handling of informative censoring, practical implementation tips (weight stabilization, truncation, machine‑learning for nuisance models), and recommended diagnostics to assess validity.

documents.content: Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) constructs a pseudo-population in which treatment is independent of measured confounders. In longitudinal settings one typically fits models for the conditional probability of receiving the observed treatment at each time given past treatment and covariate history, and possibly for censoring. Stabilized weights use marginal probabilities in the numerator to reduce variance. After computing cumulative weights one fits a weighted marginal structural model (often a pooled regression or marginal Cox model). Practical issues include extreme weights, which are handled by truncation or by better modeling of the treatment mechanism, and using robust or sandwich variance estimators for inference.
documents.reasoning_trace: Decided to include a focused exposition of IPTW mechanics: specify sequential treatment models, compute stabilized cumulative weights, fit a weighted marginal model, and mention variance estimation and extreme weight mitigation. Intentionally concise to serve as a partial but technically accurate description.

documents.content: Propensity score matching and stratification are common in cross-sectional causal analysis where treatment assignment is a one-time event and covariates are baseline. One estimates a single propensity score model for the probability of treatment given baseline covariates, then matches treated and control units or stratifies by score. Balance diagnostics include standardized mean differences and visual QQ plots. These methods do not directly accommodate time-varying exposures or confounders affected by prior treatment, because they condition only on baseline covariates and ignore longitudinal feedback between treatment and covariates.
documents.reasoning_trace: Included a clear description of standard propensity score matching/stratification for baseline treatments to contrast with longitudinal methods. Emphasized why these cross-sectional approaches fail when covariates evolve after treatment.

documents.content: Marginal structural models (MSMs) with IPTW are preferred when interest is in marginal, population-level effects of time-varying treatments and confounders are affected by prior treatment. Implementation: (1) specify sequential models for treatment and for censoring at each time point conditional on past covariates and treatments; (2) compute stabilized weights as the ratio of marginal to conditional probabilities and take products over time; (3) inspect weight distribution and truncate extreme weights if needed; (4) fit a weighted marginal model (pooled regression or marginal Cox) using robust SEs. The parametric g-formula estimates contrasts by modeling the conditional outcome process given full history, then simulating outcomes under fixed treatment regimes; it can be more efficient if outcome models are well-specified but sensitive to model misspecification. Key assumptions for both approaches are consistency, no unmeasured confounding (sequential exchangeability), and positivity. Address positivity violations via covariate coarsening, truncation, or alternative estimators (TMLE, targeted g-computation). Diagnostics: check longitudinal covariate balance under weights, examine weight variance and truncation sensitivity, compare MSM and g-formula estimates, perform parametric goodness-of-fit for outcome models, and run quantitative bias/sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding. Use flexible learning (Super Learner) for nuisance models to reduce model dependence and bootstrap or robust methods for inference.
documents.reasoning_trace: Constructed a comprehensive comparison: when MSM/IPTW is suitable, stepwise IPTW implementation, g-formula procedure, shared assumptions, practical remedies for positivity and censoring, diagnostics, and recommendations for flexible nuisance estimation. Aimed to fully answer the multi-part query with actionable steps.

documents.content: The parametric g-formula (g-computation) proceeds by modelling the conditional distribution of the outcome given past treatment and covariate history; for discrete time one fits regression models for the outcome at each time conditional on history, then iteratively simulates counterfactual trajectories under specified treatment rules and averages predicted outcomes. Advantages include direct estimation of contrasts under specified interventions and straightforward incorporation of dynamic treatment regimes; limitations include reliance on correct specification of multiple outcome and covariate evolution models. Implementation choices include model selection, Monte Carlo sample size for simulation, and sensitivity checks for model misspecification.
documents.reasoning_trace: Wrote a focused description of parametric g-formula mechanics: outcome and history models, simulation under interventions, strengths and sensitivity to misspecification. Intended as a partial, technical complement to IPTW-focused text.

documents.content: Difference-in-differences and interrupted time series designs evaluate policy effects when a clear intervention time exists and parallel trends are plausible. DID compares pre/post changes between treated and comparison groups, relying on the parallel trends assumption; implementation includes event-study checks and clustered standard errors. Interrupted time series models the counterfactual trend absent intervention using segmented regression on repeated measures. These approaches address different identification problems than longitudinal causal inference with time-varying confounders influenced by prior treatment, and they are less suited for continuous or individualized treatment regimens evolving over time.
documents.reasoning_trace: Included an overview of DID and interrupted time series as common quasi-experimental tools for policy evaluation, clarifying their assumptions and why they are conceptually distinct from time-varying confounder methods.
